newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Bank/Portugal forecasts seen pointing to rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: Bank/Portugal forecasts seen pointing to rate cuts.

text.p: The Bank of Portugal's forecasting of a significant drop in inflation in Portugal over the next two years is a clear pointer to rate cuts and a steepening yield curve, analysts said.
They said that the forecast -- with the Bank seeing inflation at just two percent in 1998 -- underlined the attractions of investing in the short end of the Portuguese bond market (OT), they added.

"The impression is that the Bank's outlook for inflation is pretty favourable and this encourages expectations, that we already had, of rate cuts in the coming months," said analyst Jose Luiz Alzola of Salomon Brothers in London.

"The Bank is going to cut rates strongly and the gains for the market are all in the short end of the curve, strategies which take advantage of its steepening," said analyst Nuno Godinho of Deutsch Morgan Grenfell in Lisbon.

In its latest quarterly bulletin, the Bank forecast the Portuguese economy would grow 3.0-3.75 percent in 1997 after 3.3 percent last year, while inflation, as measured by the Eurostat yardstick, would slow to two percent next year from a forecast 2.25 percent in 1997.
The year-on-year inflation rate was expected to ease and then hold at around two percent until the end of the third quarter from 2.5 percent in March.
"With a year-on-year rate in April, perhaps even under two percent, the Bank has to go on cutting rates," said one investment bank analyst.
The Bank last cut its repo rate 20 basis points to 6.30 percent on April 11. Its drain (absorption) rate, which the Bank regards as its key rate, was cut 40 basis points to 5.80 percent.
"The repo rate can fall 100 basis points this year," said Godinho.
For Alzola, the traditional caution of the central bank would probably limit the rate cut to 50 basis points.
"In 1997, I could see the Bank cutting the repo to 5.50 percent and the drain rate to between 5.0 and 5.20 percent," said analyst Isabel Cabral of brokers Fincor.
But regardless of how aggressive they see the Bank being in cutting rates, analysts are unanimous in seeing a steepening of the curve as yields fall at the shorter end.
"It is not difficult to image the three-month Lisbor at five percent or even below by the end of 1997," said Godinho.
The rate was set at 5.8250 percent on Tuesday. Three month rates on the money market were between 5.75 and 5.80 percent against three month rates of 5.55 percent in Spain.
"In the short-term, there is plenty of room for yields to fall in the two to three year sector," said Alzola.
Analysts said that the spread between the two and the 10 year bonds should widen, perhaps even to 135 basis points.
The spread between the March 1999 OT and the February 2007 is currently some 105 basis points.
